title: Scripture and Tradition (CCC 80–83)
hookLine: Catholics receive God's word through both the Bible and the living handing-on

cards: A stained index card in a kitchen drawer: Grandma's recipe, in her handwriting. But the card never tells you everything. How thick the batter should look.
When to turn the heat down. The little thing she did with the spoon. You learned that by standing next to her in the kitchen.
The card and the kitchen go together; lose either one, and the dish isn't quite right. Catholics say God's word reached them something like that. Today: Scripture and Tradition.

teach.b: First, the word. Tradition comes from the Latin tradere, to hand over. It's a word about passing something from one pair of hands to the next.
Paul uses the idea about the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you." Received, delivered. Handed on.
The apostles preached before any of the New Testament was written down.
And John's Gospel ends by admitting it couldn't hold everything: Jesus did many other things, and if they were all written, the world itself couldn't contain the books.
So Catholics say the faith was passed on two ways from the start: in writing, and in the living life of the Church, its preaching, worship, and practice.
Paul tells the Thessalonians to "hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word, or by our epistle." Third, one source.
The Catechism, in paragraphs 80 to 83, says Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine wellspring and work together, like two streams from one spring.
It also draws a careful line. Capital-T Tradition is the faith handed down from the apostles. Small-t traditions, like local customs and particular devotions, can change over time.

teach.h: THAT WHICH ALSO I DELIVERED UNTO YOU.
teach.b: Orthodox Christians also hold Scripture and Holy Tradition together. Many Protestant churches teach that Scripture alone is the final authority, while still valuing the creeds and the early Church.
Catholics hold both, the card and the kitchen, and believe the faith came to them through real hands, all the way back.

how: Catholics receive Scripture and Tradition together, especially in the liturgy, where the Bible is read and the ancient creeds and prayers are handed on from generation to generation.

games.q: you're one of Paul's first readers in Thessalonica. what does he tell you to hold onto?
o: only what I write to you
the traditions you've learned, by word or by letter
games.why: "hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word, or by our epistle": both the spoken and the written.

practice: Ask who handed faith, or the question of God, to you: a parent teaching you to pray, a teacher, a friend who brought you to church, a book, a stranger.
Picture that person's hands, then whoever handed it to them, and to them, back and back, a long chain of hands with you as one link. If you pray, you can thank God for each one you can name.

wordCard.voice: Tradition. From the Latin for handing over: the faith passed down from the apostles in the living life of the Church, together with Scripture. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a handing over, from tradere, to hand over.

carryVoice: Your line: handed on. Received, delivered, from one pair of hands to the next. Day two hundred ninety-three, done.
